summary: Presents an approach for building core Virtual Private Network services in a service provider's MPLS backbone. It is an informational architecture description.

eli5.summary: A phone company can carve one big network into private networks for different customers. This explains one way to do that.

questions: how do virtual routers discover each other
subtitle: How service providers carve private networks out of a shared MPLS backbone

tldr.problem: Service providers need to offer Virtual Private Network services to multiple customers using a shared backbone network, while keeping each customer's data isolated and providing a dedicated router experience.
tldr.mechanism: Create a virtual router instance for each customer inside the provider's edge routers, using MPLS label-switching for data forwarding and automatic neighbor discovery via multicast-emulated LANs.
tldr.outcome: Customers get logically independent routing domains that behave like dedicated physical routers, but the provider reuses physical hardware across multiple VPNs.

today: RFC 2917 is an Informational document describing an architectural approach developed before RFC 2547 (BGP/MPLS VPNs) became the standard for provider-managed VPNs. While this document presents useful architectural principles around virtual routers and multicast-based neighbor discovery, the BGP-based approach defined in RFC 2547 became more widely adopted in production networks.

sections.title: Building VPN Services with Virtual Routers
sections.content:
RFC 2917 presents an approach for service providers to offer Virtual Private Network (VPN) services using Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) in the backbone. The core idea is the virtual router: instead of buying a dedicated physical router for each customer, a service provider's edge device houses multiple virtual routers, one per customer VPN.

From the customer's perspective, a virtual router works like a physical router. It can run any combination of routing protocols (OSPF, RIP, BGP), maintain independent routing tables, and be configured and monitored just like dedicated hardware. But behind the scenes, multiple virtual routers share physical resources on the same physical device.
sections.eli5: Imagine a hotel giving each guest a private desk that only they can see and use, but all the desks are in the same room managed by the hotel.

sections.title: Architecture: Virtual Routers and the Emulated LAN
sections.content:
Each VPN gets a VPNID, a unique identifier within the service provider's network. Virtual routers reside at the edges of the service provider's cloud (at Service Provider Edge Devices, or SPEDs). When a customer operates multiple sites, each site connects to a SPED with its own virtual router instance.

To let these virtual routers discover each other and communicate, the architecture uses a clever trick: an emulated LAN. Instead of physical Ethernet cables, this LAN is implemented using IP multicast within the provider's backbone. Each VPN is assigned a multicast address from the administratively scoped range. Virtual routers listen on this multicast address, allowing them to exchange ARP packets, routing updates, and other control traffic as if they were on the same physical LAN.
sections.eli5: The virtual routers don't really sit on the same cable. They use a pretend LAN that works through the phone company's network using special multicast addresses.

sections.title: Configuration and Control
sections.content:
Layer 1 and Layer 2 entities (physical links, frame relay DLCIs, ATM VPI/VCIs, and LSPs) are owned and managed by the service provider. In contrast, Layer 3 (IP interfaces, routing protocols, routing policies) belongs to the customer. This separation means customers can configure their virtual routers to achieve any routing design they need—intranets, extranets, traffic engineering—without modifying existing routing protocols.

A Virtual Router Console (VRC) provides management and troubleshooting just like a physical router console. Customers can use standard tools like ping and traceroute against their own routing domains, and network administrators can monitor SNMP objects and routing tables. Security mechanisms ensure customers only access their own virtual router configuration, not the physical network layer.
sections.eli5: The customer picks an address and some routing rules for their part of the network, and the phone company handles the actual cables and hardware.

sections.title: Data Forwarding Methods
sections.content:
The RFC defines multiple forwarding strategies, in order of preference. The highest priority is policy-based forwarding, allowing customers to define fine-grained traffic handling rules. Second, a service provider can configure a private Label Switched Path (LSP) dedicated to a single VPN, optionally with bandwidth reservations and Quality of Service (QoS) characteristics. Third, a best-effort shared public LSP carries VPN traffic when no private LSP is available. The VPNID embedded in the label stack ensures packets reach the correct customer at the egress point.

This flexibility lets service providers offer differentiated services: premium customers get dedicated LSPs with QoS, while others share public LSPs with best-effort delivery.
sections.eli5: The phone company can send a customer's data through a fast priority lane, a medium shared lane, or a basic best-effort route, depending on what the customer paid for.

sections.title: Security and Isolation
sections.content:
Data isolation is guaranteed by separate forwarding tables and label stacks. Packets from different VPNs are encapsulated with different VPNID labels, so a packet from VPN A cannot leak into VPN B's forwarding path. Routing security comes from maintaining independent routing databases per virtual router, preventing one customer's router from learning about another's topology.

Configuration security is enforced by access controls on the Virtual Router Console. Only authorized personnel for a given VPN can access Layer 3 configuration for that VPN; they cannot reach physical network resources. Management authentication (password, RADIUS) is supported just like on a physical router.
sections.eli5: Each customer's data travels in a sealed envelope with their VPN's label. One customer cannot see another customer's routing tables or network plans.
